interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the whole grid and its F-shaped flag follow, the origin staying fixed and the matrix's two columns changing, when you drag the tips of i and j to where they land.
interactive.title: Drag where i and j land
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture. The picture is a squared grid of the plane. Its origin is ringed, and an F-shaped flag is drawn on it. The F looks different in a mirror, so a flip shows at once. Two arrows start at the origin. Arrow i goes one square across, to (1, 0). Arrow j goes one square up, to (0, 1). Arrow i is blue and arrow j is ink. Their names sit in teal beside their tips. A faint copy of the starting grid stays behind.

The rule is the mix of columns you met in What a matrix is. A matrix times (1, 0) takes 1 lot of column 1 and none of column 2. So i lands on column 1. In the same way, j lands on column 2. Any point (x, y) is x lots of i plus y lots of j. So it lands on x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2. Every grid line and every corner of the flag is carried that way. Each step along a grid line adds the same arrow. Lines running across add column 1 at every step. Lines running up add column 2. So the lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, unless the move squashes them flat. The origin is no lots of anything, so it stays put.

The matrix is written beside the picture, or under it on a phone. It is large enough to read at 360 px. i's landing spot runs down column 1, and j's runs down column 2. A dragged tip snaps to whole squares.

The screens.
- 1, the matrix [2 −1; 1 1], played from the do-nothing grid. i slides to (2, 1) and the grid follows. Column 2 stays faint, because j has not moved yet. The sum 1 × column 1 + 0 × column 2 is written out.
- 2, a puzzle. Where does j land under [2 −1; 1 1]? It offers (−1, 1), (1, 1) and (2, 1). After Check, j slides there.
- 3, the point (1, 2), tracked as a dot. It lands on 1 lot of (2, 1) plus 2 lots of (−1, 1), drawn nose to tail. That is (0, 3).
- 4, a puzzle. Where does (3, 1) land under the same matrix? It offers (5, 4), (7, −2) and (6, 3). The chain is drawn only after Check.
- 5, both tips free to drag. Buttons offer Stretch [2 0; 0 3], Turn, Mirror [−1 0; 0 1], Shear [1 1; 0 1] and Squash. On a narrow phone they wrap onto more lines without splitting a word. Put the tips back on (1, 0) and (0, 1), and you get the do-nothing matrix [1 0; 0 1]. Then nothing moves. Its still is the mirror, read as: the mirror [−1 0; 0 1] sends i to (−1, 0) and leaves j, so the F faces the other way.
- 6, a puzzle from picture to matrix. The grid has already moved, with i on (3, 1) and j on (0, 2). It offers [3 0; 1 2], [3 1; 0 2] and [0 3; 2 1].
- 7, the turn. An angle slider runs from 0° to 360° in steps of 15°, and opens at 30°. i's tip runs round the unit circle at (cos θ, sin θ). j's tip stays a quarter turn ahead, at (−sin θ, cos θ). The matrix reads [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ], with its values to two decimal places. At 30° that is [0.87 −0.5; 0.5 0.87]. Its still is 30°, read as: turned 30°, i lands on (0.87, 0.5), and j lands a quarter turn ahead, on (−0.5, 0.87).
- 8, a puzzle from matrix to picture. Which flag does [0 −1; 1 0] make? It offers the F turned a quarter anticlockwise, turned a quarter clockwise, and flipped over the line y = x. Each is a small drawing with those words under it.
- 9, the squash [2 1; 4 2]. i lands on (2, 4) and j on (1, 2). Both sit on one line through the origin. The grid squashes down onto that line, and the flag becomes a short line.
- 10, a puzzle. Which matrix squashes the plane onto a line? The matrix shows question marks until you check. It offers [1 3; 2 6], [1 3; 6 2] and [3 0; 0 2].
- 11, a mixed puzzle. Where does (2, 1) land under the quarter turn [0 −1; 1 0]? It offers (−1, 2), (1, −2) and (−2, 1).
- 12, a mixed puzzle. Which move can no 2 by 2 matrix make? It offers sliding the flag 3 squares right, turning it a half turn, and mirroring it in the up axis, the line x = 0. The answer is the slide. The origin is no lots of anything, so it stays put.

Some screens show an idea, and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, which wrap onto more lines on a narrow phone. A wrong pick is drawn, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The grid shows only a small patch of the plane. The plane goes on for ever in every direction, and every point of it moves. Dragged tips snap to whole squares to keep the numbers easy. But a landing spot can be any point, as the turn's are. A 3 by 3 matrix with an extra coordinate can slide the whole plane. This picture does not show that. A 3 by 3 matrix also moves space in the same way, with a third arrow k.

explain.text:
A 2 by 2 matrix can do more than hold two equations. It can move every point of the plane at once. Its two columns say where the arrows i and j land. Every other point follows from those two.

The matrix sends i and j to its own columns.[^1] Remember the mix of columns? A matrix times a column of amounts is x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2. The arrow i is (1, 0), one square across. So the matrix times i is 1 lot of column 1 and none of column 2. That is column 1 itself. In the same way, j is (0, 1), so it lands on column 2.

Every other point is built from i and j. The point (x, y) is x lots of i plus y lots of j. So it lands on x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2.[^2] Take [2 −1; 1 1]. Here i lands on (2, 1), and j lands on (−1, 1). So the point (1, 2) lands on 1 lot of (2, 1) plus 2 lots of (−1, 1). That is (0, 3).

The grid stays a grid. Each step along a grid line adds the same arrow. Lines running across add column 1 at every step. Lines running up add column 2. So the grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, unless the move squashes them flat. The origin is no lots of anything, so it never moves. A move of the whole plane like this is called a [[linear transformation]]. Four numbers describe it completely, because they are just two landing spots.

The landing spots go down the columns, not across the rows. Write them across as rows instead, and you usually get a different move. [2 1; −1 1] sends i to (2, −1), not (2, 1).

Named moves have named landing spots. A stretch keeps i and j on their axes but changes their lengths. [2 0; 0 3] is one. A mirror such as [−1 0; 0 1] sends i to (−1, 0) and keeps j. So the F faces the other way. A [[shear]] such as [1 1; 0 1] keeps i and slides j along to (1, 1). The squares lean like a pushed stack of paper.

A turn anticlockwise through θ sends i to (cos θ, sin θ). That is the tip of the arm on the unit circle. A quarter turn anticlockwise sends an arrow's across part up and its up part to the left. So (a, b) becomes (−b, a). j starts a quarter turn ahead of i, so it lands on (−sin θ, cos θ).

Sometimes both landing spots fall on one line through the origin. Then every mix of them does too, and the whole plane is squashed flat onto that line. If both land on the origin, the plane is squashed onto the origin alone.

**A 2 by 2 matrix moves the whole plane, and its two columns are where i and j land.**[^1]

analogy.text: Picture marking out fixings on a board, measuring from one corner. Each mark is so many steps along one tape and so many steps up another. Now lay the two tapes at a slant, or use a tape with longer steps. Every mark you set out moves with them. You only need to know where each tape's first step ends. That is enough to find every mark.
analogy.breaks: The board itself never stretches or turns. Only the marks you set out from the tapes move. A matrix moves the plane itself, so every point of it shifts at once. It can even squash the whole plane flat onto one line.

practice.text:
- Follow i: find where (1, 0) lands. Write it down column 1.
- Follow j: find where (0, 1) lands. Write it down column 2.
- To move any point (x, y), take x lots of column 1 plus y lots of column 2.
- Check one easy point by drawing it.

**Rule of thumb:** Columns are landing spots, and i's comes first.

**Worked example:** A quarter turn anticlockwise sends i to (0, 1) and j to (−1, 0). So its matrix is [0 −1; 1 0]. The point (3, 2) lands on 3 lots of (0, 1) plus 2 lots of (−1, 0). That is (−2, 3). Check it by turning the point in your head. A point 3 across and 2 up ends 3 up and 2 to the left after a quarter turn.

**The turn anticlockwise through θ** is [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ]. To check the minus sits in the right corner, put θ = 90°. That gives [0 −1; 1 0], which sends i straight up.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing a landing spot across a row. [2 1; −1 1] sends i to (2, −1), not (2, 1).
- Putting i's landing spot in column 2.
- Putting the turn's minus in the wrong corner. [0 1; −1 0] turns clockwise.
- Expecting a 2 by 2 matrix to slide a shape. The origin is no lots of anything, so it never moves.
